spec.full_target: Let n,m be positive integers, u:R^n×(0,∞)→R^m jointly smooth, and q a unit vector. Assume |u(x,r)|=1; u_tt−Δ_xu=a u pointwise for some real a; and on every compact time interval u=q outside a compact spatial set uniformly in time. Define e=|u_t|²+Σ|u_xj|² and E=∫R^n e dx. Prove e(·,r) integrable, E differentiable, and E'(r)=0 for every r>0; no endpoint assertion at zero.
spec.conclusion: For every r>0, e(·,r) is Lebesgue integrable, E is differentiable at r, and E'(r)=0.

propositions.statement: For every r>0, e(·,r) is Lebesgue integrable, E is differentiable at r, and E'(r)=0.

argument.text: Fix r0>0 and choose a compact interval J about it inside (0,∞). H003 gives compact C_J outside which u=q throughout J. Smoothness implies u_t and each spatial derivative vanish outside C_J and on its boundary by continuity. Thus e(·,r0) is continuous and compactly supported. M001 applies, since Euclidean Lebesgue measure is finite on compact sets and its opens are measurable, proving integrability.

Choose a closed box B containing C_J. On B×J, e_t is continuous. This product is compact, so M004 gives uniform continuity of e_t there. For each x∈B, M002 applied to t↦e(x,t) expresses its time difference quotient as the average of e_t on the intervening interval. Uniform continuity makes those quotients converge uniformly in x to e_t(x,r0). The box has finite measure, so the integrals converge as well. Since E(t)=∫_B e(x,t)dt on J, E is differentiable at r0 with derivative ∫_B e_t(x,r0)dx.

Differentiation gives e_t=2u_t·u_tt+2Σ_j u_j·∂_j u_t. For each j let g_j=u_t·u_j at time r0; it is smooth and compactly supported. Its derivative is (∂_j u_t)·u_j+u_t·u_jj and is integrable by M001. Identify R^n with R×R^(n−1) by coordinate permutation; Lebesgue measures are S-finite and the coordinate map preserves integrability, so M003 gives Fubini. For fixed remaining coordinates apply M002 to g_j on [−L,L] containing its support; the integral of ∂_j g_j is the zero endpoint difference. Thus ∫(∂_j u_t)·u_j=−∫u_t·u_jj. Summing yields E'(r0)=2∫u_t·(u_tt−Δ_xu). Differentiating H001 gives u·u_t=0; H002 says acceleration is a scalar multiple of u, so the integrand vanishes pointwise. Consequently E'(r0)=0.
Since r0>0 was arbitrary, all three claims hold for every positive time; no assertion is made at zero.
